before.claim: The measure $d\nu_\mu$ is sigma-finite by [F9], and $\omega_\mu$ and $k_j$ are finite measurable multipliers by [F2]. Applying [F5] with one-particle multiplier vector $(1,\omega_\mu,-k_1,-k_2,-k_3)$ gives the self-adjoint scalar operators $N_s,H_s,P_{s,j}$. On sector $n$, their multipliers are $n$, $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, and $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$. Squaring these multipliers and integrating against the completed product measure yields exactly the stated domains.

The Dirac data in [F6] satisfy the measurable, finite-multiplier hypotheses of [F7], and [F16] supplies the complementary orthogonal projections and closed ranges required by that carrier. The one-particle measure is sigma-finite: each of the two species copies of R^3 is the countable union of bounded balls with finite Lebesgue measure. Let Y_m be the two species copies restricted to the ball of radius m; each Y_m has finite measure. For fixed n, the product sets Y_m^n have finite product measure and cover X^n as m grows. Their countable union over n and m is a sigma-finite cover of the Fock direct-sum measure. The particle and antiparticle sector multipliers are therefore self-adjoint on the maximal domains in [F7], which are the displayed square-integrability conditions for $H_D$ and each $P_{D,j}$. The field boundedness and equal-time CAR are exactly the inspected interfaces in [F8].

For real $f$, [F3] identifies the scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ with $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$. The Hilbert space $H_\mu$ is separable by [F13], so the hypothesis of the Segal-domain result [F4] holds. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar $\sqrt2$ does not change an operator domain; hence the closure is self-adjoint on the domain in [F4] with $h=K_\mu f$. If $K_\mu f=0$, both operators are zero on all Fock space.

For a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $|\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle|\le\|A\Psi\|<\infty$. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, this expectation is real. The vector $A\Psi-\langle A\rangle_\Psi\Psi$ belongs to the Hilbert space because both terms do, so its norm and the stated variance are finite without requiring $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. By [F14], a product $AB$ acts only on vectors $\Psi\in D(B)$ for which $B\Psi\in D(A)$; it is not defined merely because both $A$ and $B$ separately exist on a common dense core.

Choose $b_d$ from [F18] for $d=3,4$. Put
$Z_d=\int b_d(x)\,d^dx$ and $\rho_d=Z_d^{-1}b_d$.
The integral is finite because $0\le b_d\le1$ and its support lies in a
bounded ball, and it is positive because $b_d=1$ on a ball of positive
volume. Every derivative of $b_d$ is continuous with compact support, so
all its coordinate-weighted derivatives are bounded. Thus $\rho_d$ is
Schwartz, nonnegative, nonzero, and has integral one. In particular
$0<\|\rho_d\|_2<\infty$. Define
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\rho_d(x)\,d^dx$.
The integral triangle inequality gives $|\widehat\rho_d(\xi)|\le\int\rho_d=1$;
dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\rho_d$, gives
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)\to1$ as $\xi\to0$.
Set $\rho=\rho_4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)=\varepsilon^{-4}\rho_4((x-x_0)/\varepsilon)$. For every Schwartz test $\phi$, change of variables and dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\|\phi\|_\infty\rho_4(y)$, give $\int\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$, so this is a point-mass approximation. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in H_\mu^+$ the same change of variables gives
$$K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)=e^{ip\circ x_0}\widehat\rho_4\bigl(\varepsilon(-p^0,\mathbf p)\bigr).$$
Thus $K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for every fixed shell momentum and $|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)|\le1$. The shell measure has infinite total mass: in radial coordinates, for $r\ge\max(1,\mu)$, $\omega_\mu(r)\le\sqrt2\,r$, so its radial density is bounded below by a positive constant times $r\,dr$, whose integral diverges. Fatou's lemma [F11] therefore gives $\liminf_{\varepsilon_m\downarrow0}\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|^2\ge\int_{H_\mu^+}1\,d\nu_\mu=\infty$. By [F1, F3] and the creation formula on the vacuum, $\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0})\Omega\|=\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|$, so these vacuum vectors have no finite-norm point-field limit.

The scalar one-particle space contains a unit vector $e$, for example a normalized indicator of an annulus $1<|\mathbf k|<2$, whose shell measure is finite and positive by [F2]. The symmetric vectors $e^{\otimes n}$ are unit vectors in mutually orthogonal sectors. Put $C=(\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4})^{-1/2}$ and $\Psi_n=Cn^{-2}e^{\otimes n}$. By [F15], $\sum n^{-4}$ converges and is positive, so $C$ is well-defined and $\Psi$ is normalized. Also by [F15], $\sum n^{-2}<\infty$, so $\Psi\in D(N_s)$ and $N_s\Psi=(Cn^{-1}e^{\otimes n})_{n\ge1}$ is a Fock vector. Its image under one more application of $N_s$ would have squared norm $C^2\sum_{n\ge1}1=\infty$, so $N_s\Psi\notin D(N_s)$. By the composition-domain rule [F14] with $A=B=N_s$, $\Psi\notin D(N_s^2)$. Its mean and variance are finite by 2.2.

Fix a unit spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\rho_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\varepsilon)z$. For every spatial Schwartz test, change of variables and [F10] show that its pairing with $u_\varepsilon$ tends to the test's value at $\mathbf x_0$ times $z$, while $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2=\varepsilon^{-3/2}\|\rho_3\|_2\to\infty$. By [F16], choose countable dense sets in the two Dirac energy ranges. Conjugating the negative-range dense set preserves density, and the Cartesian product of the two dense sets is countable and dense in the Hilbert direct sum. Therefore the one-particle space for the CAR Fock representation is separable and [F17] applies. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. The adjoint identity swaps $x$ and $y$, so the same two-vector supremum equals $\|A_\varepsilon^\dagger\|$. For bounded operators $X,Y$, each unit $\xi$ satisfies $\|XY\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\|$ and $\|(X+Y)\xi\|\le\|X\xi\|+\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|+\|Y\|$; taking suprema gives product submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality. Applying these inequalities to the CAR identity yields $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon\|\le2\|A_\varepsilon\|^2$. Thus $\|A_\varepsilon\|\ge\|u_\varepsilon\|_2/\sqrt2\to\infty$, excluding a bounded equal-time point-field norm limit.

Assume Countable Choice and use the scalar and Dirac free-field constructions of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] and [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]] with their current draft hypotheses, including the Dirac projection and CAR inputs in [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. For a real scalar test $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$, $\overline{\Phi_\mu(f)}=\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$ is self-adjoint on the exact domain given by [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. On scalar bosonic Fock space, $N_s=d\Gamma(1)$, $H_s=d\Gamma(\omega_\mu)$, and $P_{s,j}=d\Gamma(-k_j)$ are the maximal real multipliers of [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]; in particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\},$$
and the Hamiltonian and momentum domains are exactly the square-integrability domains of the sums of their one-particle multipliers.

On the specified Dirac Fock space, spacetime-smeared fields $\Psi(F)$ are bounded, while the translation generators $H_D,P_{D,j}$ have the exact maximal domains and joint PVM stated in [[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]]. For any one of these self-adjoint real-multiplier operators $A$, a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$ has finite mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and finite variance
$$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2.$$
Membership in $D(A)$ suffices for finite variance and does not require $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. A product $AB\Psi$ is defined only when $\Psi\in D(B)$ and $B\Psi\in D(A)$, as specified in [[lem-nrqm-uncertainty-schrodinger-robertson-anticommutator-bound]].

For the scalar point limit, fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^4$ and real tests $f_\varepsilon\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$, such that $\int f_\varepsilon(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$ for every Schwartz test $\phi$ and $K_\mu f_\varepsilon(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for $\nu_\mu$-almost every shell momentum. Then $\|\Phi_\mu(f_\varepsilon)\Omega\|\to\infty$. A sufficient condition for both convergences is $\int f_\varepsilon=1$, $\sup_\varepsilon\|f_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty$, and $\int_{|x-x_0|\ge\delta}|f_\varepsilon(x)|\,d^4x\to0$ for each $\delta>0$. This includes all nonnegative normalized Schwartz approximate identities with mass concentrating at $x_0$, as well as signed families satisfying that condition; weak distributional convergence alone is not substituted for convergence of the mass-shell Fourier restriction. For the equal-time Dirac CAR field, fix $\mathbf x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and $z_0\in\mathbb C^4\setminus\{0\}$. For every family $u_\varepsilon\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$ satisfying $\int h(\mathbf x)^\dagger u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\to h(\mathbf x_0)^\dagger z_0$ for each spinor Schwartz test $h$, the bounded equal-time smeared operators satisfy $\|\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)\|_{\rm op}\to\infty$ at each fixed time $t$. Thus neither construction gives a point-field value in the indicated norm topology. The supplied free-field results define only smeared fields and do not define coincident diagonal products.

after.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.3 explicitly include the massless shell μ=0 and its measure-zero apex.

before.claim: By [F5], $\Lambda$ preserves $\eta$ and sends a future null vector $p$ to a future null vector $\Lambda p$. It maps $p^\perp$ onto $(\Lambda p)^\perp$ and $\mathbb Cp$ onto $\mathbb C\Lambda p$, so it induces a well-defined map on the quotient fiber. The induced form is preserved because $\eta(\Lambda v,\Lambda w)=\eta(v,w)$; hence the fiber map is an isometry. The map $T_p$ is independent of the representative: replacing $\epsilon$ by $\epsilon+cp$ changes its value by $c(\mathbf k-(\mathbf k/\omega)\omega)=0$. For $\epsilon\in p^\perp$, $\mathbf k\cdot T_p[\epsilon]=0$; its pairing is the positive quotient pairing of [F1]. The lift $\epsilon=(0,\sqrt{2\omega}\,u(\mathbf k))$ for transverse $u$ proves surjectivity, and $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$ gives $\int\|T_p[s(p)]\|^2d\nu=\int\|u(\mathbf k)\|^2d^3\mathbf k$. Thus the stated section identification is well-defined and unitary. Applying two Lorentz maps successively gives the representation composition law.

The component identification of [F3] uses $X=\mathbb R^3\times\{1,2,3\}$ with Lebesgue measure times counting measure; $X$ is sigma-finite because the boxes $[-m,m]^3\times\{1,2,3\}$ have finite measure by [F8]. The finite measurable map $\boldsymbol\omega(\mathbf k,j)=(|\mathbf k|,-\mathbf k)$ lets us apply [F3]. It gives the PVM $\mathsf E(B)$ whose $n$-particle multiplier is $\mathbf1_{\{(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)\in B\}}$, with vacuum multiplier $\mathbf1_B(0)$, and it gives the maximal componentwise multiplier domains. By [F7], $P_T(\mathbf k)$ is pointwise self-adjoint and idempotent, so it commutes with each scalar multiplier; its tensor powers commute with the n-particle PVM and multiplier. The symmetric transverse sector is reducing, so restriction preserves the maximal domain, which for the energy is exactly $D(H_E)$ displayed in the Statement.

For the boost $B_n(\chi)$ in [F2], put $\beta=\tanh\chi$ and $\gamma=\cosh\chi$, so $|\beta|<1$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. In Euclidean unit direction $n$ [F5], its spatial cone coordinates satisfy

Each joint multiplier value $(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)$ lies in $\overline V_+$ by the triangle inequality [F9], so the PVM vanishes outside that closed cone. Fix a nonzero $\mathbf k_0$ and the boundary point $(|\mathbf k_0|,-\mathbf k_0)$. Choose $v\in\mathbb R^3$ not parallel to $\mathbf k_0$. By [F7], $P_T(\mathbf k_0)v\ne0$, and continuity gives a bounded open momentum neighborhood $V$ of $\mathbf k_0$, disjoint from zero, on which $\|P_T(\mathbf k)v\|$ is bounded below by a positive constant. Given any open neighborhood $G$ of $(|\mathbf k_0|,-\mathbf k_0)$, shrink $V$ so the map $\mathbf k\mapsto(|\mathbf k|,-\mathbf k)$ sends $V$ into $G$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. Give the proper orthochronous Lorentz group its matrix topology: the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb R^{16}$ with Euclidean matrix norm $\|A\|_{\rm mat}=(\sum_{i,j=0}^3|A_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous for this topology, meaning $\|U_\Lambda s-U_{\Lambda_0}s\|\to0$ for every section $s$ as $\|\Lambda-\Lambda_0\|_{\rm mat}\to0$. Its bosonic Fock lift is strongly continuous for the same topology. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation for $a=(a^0,\mathbf a)\in\mathbb R^4$ has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has the joint PVM $\mathsf E$ whose $n$-particle sector acts by multiplication by $\mathbf1_{\{(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_{r=1}^n\mathbf k_r)\in B\}}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; on the vacuum it acts by $\mathbf1_B(0)$. Define its joint spectrum to be
$$\operatorname{supp}(\mathsf E):=\{q\in\mathbb R^4:\mathsf E(U)\ne0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }q\}.$$
Then this joint spectrum is the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. In the product realization of the sectors in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]], on sector $n$ the energy operator multiplies by $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and has the exact maximal domain
$$D(H_E)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|\right)^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$
with the vacuum component unrestricted; here $\Psi_n$ is the symmetric transverse wavefunction in the product realization and the norm is the product-fiber Hilbert norm. Each momentum operator $P_j$ multiplies by $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$ and has maximal domain
$$D(P_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left|\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}\right|^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$
again with unrestricted vacuum component. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.
(d) [Moments] $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$,

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$** ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

after.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.
(d) [Moments] $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$,

Fix an inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and identify its vector coordinates with $\mathbb R^4$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n_B$ and $\chi\in\mathbb R$, define the boost $B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)$ by $B e_0=\cosh\chi\,e_0+\sinh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, $B\mathbf n_B=\sinh\chi\,e_0+\cosh\chi\,\mathbf n_B$, and $Bw=w$ for every $w$ Euclidean-orthogonal to $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n_B)$. Every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], admits $\Lambda=B_{\mathbf n_B}(\chi)R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$, where $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)$ fixes the time axis and $\mathbf n_R$, and sends $\mathbf v_\perp$ to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n_R\times\mathbf v_\perp$ on the orthogonal plane, where $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n_R)\mathbf n_R$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$; the cross product is [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $\Lambda e_0=e_0$, choose $\chi=0$ and $R_{\mathbf n_R}(\theta)=\Lambda$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j=(j_1,j_2,j_3)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ and use $\mathcal H_T$ and $P_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. For $\omega=|\mathbf k|$ and $\mathbf k\ne0$, define
$$g_j(\mathbf k)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\, P_T(\mathbf k)\int_{\mathbb R^4}j(x)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^4x.$$
Then $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$. On the finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$, the smeared transverse potential is
$$A_T(j)=a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j).$$
Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation for $a=(a^0,\mathbf a)\in\mathbb R^4$ has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has the joint PVM $\mathsf E$ whose $n$-particle sector acts by multiplication by $\mathbf1_{\{(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_{r=1}^n\mathbf k_r)\in B\}}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; on the vacuum it acts by $\mathbf1_B(0)$. Define its joint spectrum to be
$$\operatorname{supp}(\mathsf E):=\{q\in\mathbb R^4:\mathsf E(U)\ne0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }q\}.$$
Then this joint spectrum is the closed future cone

continuous polarization frame over all momentum directions is chosen. Adopt

Hamiltonian

self-adjoint domain and the unitary mass-cone action are those in the
mathematical supplier [[lem-qft-photon-covariance-spectrum]]. The actual
smeared field-strength distributions and bounded Weyl operators are those
constructed in [[lem-qft-photon-local-weyl-observables]]; a pointwise
potential or field-strength operator is not asserted to exist. These
mathematical suppliers are draft carriers with mixed current Step 1 status: the
transverse-space, null-quotient, covariance-spectrum, framework-units, and
C01 measurement carriers have current ready records; the local-Weyl carrier is
escalated through its field-strength prerequisite. Readiness records are not
independent approval, and every use remains conditional on the exact statement
and proof supplied.

For the physical interpretation of an actually constructed state and a
supplied normalized measurement instrument, use
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]: Born probabilities are
assigned only to that specified model and instrument. This postulate records
the model's free Maxwell quanta as photons. It does not assert that the
model has been empirically confirmed, and it introduces no interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, LSZ limit,
asymptotic completeness, or nonperturbative continuum limit. In calculations
using an indefinite four-polarization auxiliary space, only the positive
transverse model or its separately constructed null quotient is physical;
four auxiliary components are not four positive photon states.

statement.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}$, so the effective Clifford metric is
$-\eta$. In a supplied free Dirac model the displayed equation is
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has joint spectrum the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. The energy is the nonnegative sector multiplier $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ with the exact maximal square-integrability domain on each sector and square-summability over sectors. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. This unit conversion alone does not identify a
Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write
$\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta$. The effective Clifford metric is $-\eta$.
A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field
equation.

If a selected model supplies a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$ as in
[[def-hilbert-space]], a complex-linear Hamiltonian operator
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with model-specified linear domain $D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$
and SI energy unit joules, and an evolution family $U(t):\mathscr H\to\mathscr H$
for $t\in I\subseteq\mathbb R$ in seconds, the convention is
$U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad
D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies these domains and the evolution; this dictionary constructs
no Hamiltonian, evolution family, or field representation. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It
asserts only matrix-element continuity and the stated linear maps; all further
operator properties, locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is
dimensionless; there is no universal test-function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. Give the proper orthochronous Lorentz group its matrix topology: the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb R^{16}$ with Euclidean matrix norm $\|A\|_{\rm mat}=(\sum_{i,j=0}^3|A_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous for this topology, meaning $\|U_\Lambda s-U_{\Lambda_0}s\|\to0$ for every section $s$ as $\|\Lambda-\Lambda_0\|_{\rm mat}\to0$. Its bosonic Fock lift is strongly continuous for the same topology. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation for $a=(a^0,\mathbf a)\in\mathbb R^4$ has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Its bosonic Fock lift has the joint PVM $\mathsf E$ whose $n$-particle sector acts by multiplication by $\mathbf1_{\{(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_{r=1}^n\mathbf k_r)\in B\}}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; on the vacuum it acts by $\mathbf1_B(0)$. Define its joint spectrum to be
$$\operatorname{supp}(\mathsf E):=\{q\in\mathbb R^4:\mathsf E(U)\ne0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }q\}.$$
Then this joint spectrum is the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. In the product realization of the sectors in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]], on sector $n$ the energy operator multiplies by $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and has the exact maximal domain
$$D(H_E)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|\right)^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$
with the vacuum component unrestricted; here $\Psi_n$ is the symmetric transverse wavefunction in the product realization and the norm is the product-fiber Hilbert norm. Each momentum operator $P_j$ multiplies by $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$ and has maximal domain
$$D(P_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left|\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}\right|^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$
again with unrestricted vacuum component. These are mathematical free-field representation statements.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, an inertial length-coordinate chart
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$, $x^0=ct$, and coordinates measured in metres, as specified
by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write
$\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The mass-shell parameter $\mu\ge0$ has
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same unit. For a
massive species, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the separately
admitted massless branch of the mathematical free-field construction. Thus
$\hbar c\omega_\mu$ is physical energy and $\hbar\mathbf k$ is physical
momentum. The natural-unit action is written $S/\hbar$.

The scalar one-particle space is
$\mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, where
$H_\mu^+=\{(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3,\ \omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0\}$ and
$d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$; at $\mu=0$ the
measure-zero apex $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted. These are the shell conventions
of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]].

For a smooth real classical scalar $\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$
with the canonical free-field length degree $-1$, adopt
$$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n}+\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$
For a smooth commuting classical Dirac spinor
$\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ with canonical free-field length
degree $-3/2$, put $\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}=\psi_{\mathrm n}^\dagger\beta$ and
use the Clifford convention
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Adopt
$$\frac{S_D}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}\,d^4x.$$
The smooth classical variables in these functionals commute; no Grassmann
algebra or path-integral construction is being adopted. These formulas specify
local action densities: for arbitrary smooth global fields the total
integrals need not converge. Only compactly supported variations are used;
the action difference under such a variation is an integral over a compact

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
