On scalar bosonic Fock space, $N_s=d\Gamma(1)$, $H_s=d\Gamma(\omega_\mu)$, and $P_{s,j}=d\Gamma(-k_j)$ are the maximal real multipliers of [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]; in particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\},$$
and the Hamiltonian and momentum domains are exactly the square-integrability domains of the sums of their one-particle multipliers.

On the specified Dirac Fock space, spacetime-smeared fields $\Psi(F)$ are bounded, while the translation generators $H_D,P_{D,j}$ have the exact maximal domains and joint PVM stated in [[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]]. For any one of these self-adjoint real-multiplier operators $A$, a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$ has finite mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and finite variance
$$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2.$$
Membership in $D(A)$ suffices for finite variance and does not require $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. A product $AB\Psi$ is defined only when $\Psi\in D(B)$ and $B\Psi\in D(A)$, as specified in [[lem-nrqm-uncertainty-schrodinger-robertson-anticommutator-bound]].

For the scalar point limit, fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^4$ and real tests $f_\varepsilon\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$, such that $\int f_\varepsilon(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$ for every Schwartz test $\phi$ and $K_\mu f_\varepsilon(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for $\nu_\mu$-almost every shell momentum. Then $\|\Phi_\mu(f_\varepsilon)\Omega\|\to\infty$. A sufficient condition for both convergences is $\int f_\varepsilon=1$, $\sup_\varepsilon\|f_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty$, and $\int_{|x-x_0|\ge\delta}|f_\varepsilon(x)|\,d^4x\to0$ for each $\delta>0$. This includes all nonnegative normalized Schwartz approximate identities with mass concentrating at $x_0$, as well as signed families satisfying that condition; weak distributional convergence alone is not substituted for convergence of the mass-shell Fourier restriction. For the equal-time Dirac CAR field, fix $\mathbf x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and $z_0\in\mathbb C^4\setminus\{0\}$. For every family $u_\varepsilon\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$ satisfying $\int h(\mathbf x)^\dagger u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\to h(\mathbf x_0)^\dagger z_0$ for each spinor Schwartz test $h$, the bounded equal-time smeared operators satisfy $\|\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)\|_{\rm op}\to\infty$ at each fixed time $t$. Thus neither construction gives a point-field value in the indicated norm topology. The supplied free-field results define only smeared fields and do not define coincident diagonal products.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open. For real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O)$ define
$$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2K_\mu f),$$
where the Segal normalization is exactly
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2$ on the finite-particle
domain, as in [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. This scale makes the self-adjoint generator
of $t\mapsto W_\mu(tf)$ equal to the closure $\overline{\Phi_\mu(f)}$,
whose restriction to $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is the real scalar field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the unital norm-closed operator
algebra
$$\mathfrak A_\mu(O)= \overline{\operatorname{alg}}^{\|\cdot\|} \{I,W_\mu(f),W_\mu(f)^*:f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)\}.$$
Then $O_1\subseteq O_2$ implies
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. If every difference
$x-y$, with $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, is spacelike, then every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)$ commutes with every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. These are algebraic properties of the constructed
representation; they are not empirical signaling or measurement claims.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], and the antisymmetric Fock and CAR conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. Define
$$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4):=\{F=(F_0,F_1,F_2,F_3):F_a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)\text{ for }a=0,1,2,3\},$$
with the finite-product topology generated by the scalar Schwartz seminorms on each component; $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$ and its seminorms are those of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. For $F$ in this space, define
$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
Then $u_F\in\mathcal H_D$, continuously in the Schwartz topology, and
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$$
defines a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$, antilinear in $F$. It satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle_{\mathcal H_D}I.$$
The positive and negative contraction kernels, defined as tempered distributions by their Fourier integrals, are
$$C_+(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{-i(\omega\tau-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_+(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad C_-(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{+i(\omega\tau+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_-(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}.$$
Their tested pairings give respectively $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$; their sum is the anticommutator kernel $R$ below.
Its tested free equation is $u_{(i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F}=0$. For spatial Schwartz spinors $u,v$, the equal-time field $\Psi_t(u)=c(P_+W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u})$ satisfies $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)^\dagger\}=\int u(\mathbf x)^\dagger v(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\,I$ and $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)\}=0$.

The spacetime anticommutator kernel is
$$R(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}W_D(-\tau,\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}=\partial_\tau\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x)I_4-i h_D(-i\nabla)\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x),$$
where $\Delta_\mu$ is the scalar causal commutator distribution of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. Thus the kernel is supported in the closed causal cone. Spinor tests with compact spacelike-separated supports have vanishing anticommutators with one another and with each other's adjoints. Consequently, even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions. These are mathematical properties of the specified free-field construction.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F18].

1.1 The measure $d\nu_\mu$ is sigma-finite by [F9], and $\omega_\mu$ and $k_j$ are finite measurable multipliers by [F2]. Applying [F5] with one-particle multiplier vector $(1,\omega_\mu,-k_1,-k_2,-k_3)$ gives the self-adjoint scalar operators $N_s,H_s,P_{s,j}$. On sector $n$, their multipliers are $n$, $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, and $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$. Squaring these multipliers and integrating against the completed product measure yields exactly the stated domains. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F9, given]

1.2 The Dirac data in [F6] satisfy the measurable, finite-multiplier hypotheses of [F7], and [F16] supplies the complementary orthogonal projections and closed ranges required by that carrier. The one-particle measure is sigma-finite: each of the two species copies of R^3 is the countable union of bounded balls with finite Lebesgue measure. Let Y_m be the two species copies restricted to the ball of radius m; each Y_m has finite measure. For fixed n, the product sets Y_m^n have finite product measure and cover X^n as m grows. Their countable union over n and m is a sigma-finite cover of the Fock direct-sum measure. The particle and antiparticle sector multipliers are therefore self-adjoint on the maximal domains in [F7], which are the displayed square-integrability conditions for $H_D$ and each $P_{D,j}$. The field boundedness and equal-time CAR are exactly the inspected interfaces in [F8]. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F8, F16, given]

2.1 For real $f$, [F3] identifies the scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ with $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$. The Hilbert space $H_\mu$ is separable by [F13], so the hypothesis of the Segal-domain result [F4] holds. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar $\sqrt2$ does not change an operator domain; hence the closure is self-adjoint on the domain in [F4] with $h=K_\mu f$. If $K_\mu f=0$, both operators are zero on all Fock space. [F1, F3, F4, F13, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $|\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle|\le\|A\Psi\|<\infty$. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, this expectation is real. The vector $A\Psi-\langle A\rangle_\Psi\Psi$ belongs to the Hilbert space because both terms do, so its norm and the stated variance are finite without requiring $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. By [F14], a product $AB$ acts only on vectors $\Psi\in D(B)$ for which $B\Psi\in D(A)$; it is not defined merely because both $A$ and $B$ separately exist on a common dense core. [F1, F12, F14, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

2.3 Choose $b_d$ from [F18] for $d=3,4$. Put
$Z_d=\int b_d(x)\,d^dx$ and $\rho_d=Z_d^{-1}b_d$.
The integral is finite because $0\le b_d\le1$ and its support lies in a
bounded ball, and it is positive because $b_d=1$ on a ball of positive
volume. Every derivative of $b_d$ is continuous with compact support, so
all its coordinate-weighted derivatives are bounded. Thus $\rho_d$ is
Schwartz, nonnegative, nonzero, and has integral one. In particular
$0<\|\rho_d\|_2<\infty$. Define
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\rho_d(x)\,d^dx$.
The integral triangle inequality gives $|\widehat\rho_d(\xi)|\le\int\rho_d=1$;
dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\rho_d$, gives
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)\to1$ as $\xi\to0$.
Set $\rho=\rho_4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)=\varepsilon^{-4}\rho_4((x-x_0)/\varepsilon)$. For every Schwartz test $\phi$, change of variables and dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\|\phi\|_\infty\rho_4(y)$, give $\int\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$, so this is a point-mass approximation. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in H_\mu^+$ the same change of variables gives
$$K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)=e^{ip\circ x_0}\widehat\rho_4\bigl(\varepsilon(-p^0,\mathbf p)\bigr).$$
Thus $K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for every fixed shell momentum and $|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)|\le1$. The shell measure has infinite total mass: in radial coordinates, for $r\ge\max(1,\mu)$, $\omega_\mu(r)\le\sqrt2\,r$, so its radial density is bounded below by a positive constant times $r\,dr$, whose integral diverges. Fatou's lemma [F11] therefore gives $\liminf_{\varepsilon_m\downarrow0}\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|^2\ge\int_{H_\mu^+}1\,d\nu_\mu=\infty$. By [F1, F3] and the creation formula on the vacuum, $\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0})\Omega\|=\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|$, so these vacuum vectors have no finite-norm point-field limit. More generally, suppose $f_\varepsilon$ satisfies the scalar hypotheses in the Statement. For any sequence $\varepsilon_j\to0$, Fatou [F11] applied to $|K_\mu f_{\varepsilon_j}|^2$ gives $\liminf_j\|K_\mu f_{\varepsilon_j}\|^2\ge\int1\,d\nu_\mu=\infty$. Thus the norms diverge as $\varepsilon\to0$: otherwise a bounded sequence with $\varepsilon_j<1/j$ could be selected using [A1], contradicting this conclusion. The vacuum creation identity gives the asserted field-vector norm. To verify the sufficient concentration condition, let $M=\sup_\varepsilon\|f_\varepsilon\|_1$ and let $g$ be any bounded continuous scalar function. Since $\int f_\varepsilon=1$, splitting the integral at radius $\delta$ gives $|\int f_\varepsilon(x)g(x)\,d^4x-g(x_0)|\le M\sup_{|x-x_0|<\delta}|g(x)-g(x_0)|+2\|g\|_\infty\int_{|x-x_0|\ge\delta}|f_\varepsilon(x)|\,d^4x$. First choose $\delta$ using continuity at $x_0$, then take $\varepsilon\to0$. Applying this to Schwartz $g$ and to $g(x)=e^{ip\circ x}$ proves both required limits. Every rescaling of a nonnegative normalized Schwartz profile has $M=1$ and satisfies concentration by its integrable tail; hence the general conclusion includes every such profile, not only the chosen bumps. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F9, F10, F11, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The scalar one-particle space contains a unit vector $e$, for example a normalized indicator of an annulus $1<|\mathbf k|<2$, whose shell measure is finite and positive by [F2]. The symmetric vectors $e^{\otimes n}$ are unit vectors in mutually orthogonal sectors. Put $C=(\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4})^{-1/2}$ and $\Psi_n=Cn^{-2}e^{\otimes n}$. By [F15], $\sum n^{-4}$ converges and is positive, so $C$ is well-defined and $\Psi$ is normalized. Also by [F15], $\sum n^{-2}<\infty$, so $\Psi\in D(N_s)$ and $N_s\Psi=(Cn^{-1}e^{\otimes n})_{n\ge1}$ is a Fock vector. Its image under one more application of $N_s$ would have squared norm $C^2\sum_{n\ge1}1=\infty$, so $N_s\Psi\notin D(N_s)$. By the composition-domain rule [F14] with $A=B=N_s$, $\Psi\notin D(N_s^2)$. Its mean and variance are finite by 2.2. [F1, F2, F5, F14, F15, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 Fix a unit spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\rho_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\varepsilon)z$. For every spatial Schwartz test, change of variables and [F10] show that its pairing with $u_\varepsilon$ tends to the test's value at $\mathbf x_0$ times $z$, while $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2=\varepsilon^{-3/2}\|\rho_3\|_2\to\infty$. For a general family in the Dirac Statement, set $e=z_0/\|z_0\|$ and $h_a(\mathbf x)=b_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/a)e$ for $a>0$. By [F18], this is a spinor Schwartz test, $h_a(\mathbf x_0)^\dagger z_0=\|z_0\|$, and $\|h_a\|_2=a^{3/2}\|b_3\|_2$. Given $L>0$, choose $a$ with $\|h_a\|_2<\|z_0\|/(2L)$. The assumed pairing limit then gives $|\langle h_a,u_\varepsilon\rangle_2|>\|z_0\|/2$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] implies $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2>L$. Thus every such family has $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2\to\infty$. The following operator estimate applies to either the explicit bump family or this arbitrary family. By [F16], choose countable dense sets in the two Dirac energy ranges. Conjugating the negative-range dense set preserves density, and the Cartesian product of the two dense sets is countable and dense in the Hilbert direct sum. Therefore the one-particle space for the CAR Fock representation is separable and [F17] applies. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. The adjoint identity swaps $x$ and $y$, so the same two-vector supremum equals $\|A_\varepsilon^\dagger\|$. For bounded operators $X,Y$, each unit $\xi$ satisfies $\|XY\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\|$ and $\|(X+Y)\xi\|\le\|X\xi\|+\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|+\|Y\|$; taking suprema gives product submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality. Applying these inequalities to the CAR identity yields $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon\|\le2\|A_\varepsilon\|^2$. Thus $\|A_\varepsilon\|\ge\|u_\varepsilon\|_2/\sqrt2\to\infty$, excluding a bounded equal-time point-field norm limit. [F8, F10, F12, F16, F17, F18, step 2.3, given, algebra] ∎

Their countable union over n and m is a sigma-finite cover of the Fock direct-sum measure. Therefore the one-particle space for the CAR Fock representation is separable and [F17] applies. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. The adjoint identity swaps $x$ and $y$, so the same two-vector supremum equals $\|A_\varepsilon^\dagger\|$. For bounded operators $X,Y$, each unit $\xi$ satisfies $\|XY\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\|$ and $\|(X+Y)\xi\|\le\|X\xi\|+\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|+\|Y\|$; taking suprema gives product submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality. Applying these inequalities to the CAR identity yields $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon\|\le2\|A_\varepsilon\|^2$. Thus $\|A_\varepsilon\|\ge\|u_\varepsilon\|_2/\sqrt2\to\infty$, excluding a bounded equal-time point-field norm limit. [F8, F10, F12, F16, F17, F18, step 2.3, given, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. On the future null cone write $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$, $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, $\mathbf k\ne0$, and use the measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. The fiber $p^\perp/\mathbb Cp$ has the positive quotient form of [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]]. Give the proper orthochronous Lorentz group its matrix topology: the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb R^{16}$ with Euclidean matrix norm $\|A\|_{\rm mat}=(\sum_{i,j=0}^3|A_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$. For each proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$, the action
$$[s(p)]\longmapsto[\Lambda s(\Lambda^{-1}p)]$$
is a unitary representation on the square-integrable quotient sections. It is strongly continuous for this topology, meaning $\|U_\Lambda s-U_{\Lambda_0}s\|\to0$ for every section $s$ as $\|\Lambda-\Lambda_0\|_{\rm mat}\to0$. Its bosonic Fock lift is strongly continuous for the same topology. Under the unitary identification with $\mathcal H_T$ given by
$T_p[\epsilon]:=\boldsymbol\epsilon-(\mathbf k/\omega)\epsilon^0$
and $u(\mathbf k)=T_p[s(p)]/\sqrt{2\omega}$, as in [[lem-qft-photon-null-quotient]], the free translation representation for $a=(a^0,\mathbf a)\in\mathbb R^4$ has phase $e^{i(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$. Define its joint spectrum to be
$$\operatorname{supp}(\mathsf E):=\{q\in\mathbb R^4:\mathsf E(U)\ne0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }q\}.$$
Then this joint spectrum is the closed future cone
$$\overline V_+=\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\},$$
with the vacuum at $(0,\mathbf0)$. In the product realization of the sectors in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]], on sector $n$ the energy operator multiplies by $\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|$ and has the exact maximal domain
$$D(H_E)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left(\sum_{r=1}^n|\mathbf k_r|\right)^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$

$$D(P_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(\mathbb R^3)^n}\left|\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}\right|^2\|\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)\|^2\,d^3\mathbf k_1\cdots d^3\mathbf k_n<\infty\right\},$$

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F11], the future-cone parametrization, and the componentwise Lorentz action.

1.1 By [F5], $\Lambda$ preserves $\eta$ and sends a future null vector $p$ to a future null vector $\Lambda p$. It maps $p^\perp$ onto $(\Lambda p)^\perp$ and $\mathbb Cp$ onto $\mathbb C\Lambda p$, so it induces a well-defined map on the quotient fiber. The induced form is preserved because $\eta(\Lambda v,\Lambda w)=\eta(v,w)$; hence the fiber map is an isometry. The map $T_p$ is independent of the representative: replacing $\epsilon$ by $\epsilon+cp$ changes its value by $c(\mathbf k-(\mathbf k/\omega)\omega)=0$. For $\epsilon\in p^\perp$, $\mathbf k\cdot T_p[\epsilon]=0$; its pairing is the positive quotient pairing of [F1]. The lift $\epsilon=(0,\sqrt{2\omega}\,u(\mathbf k))$ for transverse $u$ proves surjectivity, and $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$ gives $\int\|T_p[s(p)]\|^2d\nu=\int\|u(\mathbf k)\|^2d^3\mathbf k$. Thus the stated section identification is well-defined and unitary. Applying two Lorentz maps successively gives the representation composition law. [F1, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 The component identification of [F3] uses $X=\mathbb R^3\times\{1,2,3\}$ with Lebesgue measure times counting measure; $X$ is sigma-finite because the boxes $[-m,m]^3\times\{1,2,3\}$ have finite measure by [F8]. The finite measurable map $\boldsymbol\omega(\mathbf k,j)=(|\mathbf k|,-\mathbf k)$ lets us apply [F3]. It gives the PVM $\mathsf E(B)$ whose $n$-particle multiplier is $\mathbf1_{\{(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)\in B\}}$, with vacuum multiplier $\mathbf1_B(0)$, and it gives the maximal componentwise multiplier domains. By [F7], $P_T(\mathbf k)$ is pointwise self-adjoint and idempotent, so it commutes with each scalar multiplier; its tensor powers commute with the n-particle PVM and multiplier. The symmetric transverse sector is reducing, so restriction preserves the maximal domain, which for the energy is exactly $D(H_E)$ displayed in the Statement. [A1, F3, F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 For the boost $B_n(\chi)$ in [F2], put $\beta=\tanh\chi$ and $\gamma=\cosh\chi$, so $|\beta|<1$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. In Euclidean unit direction $n$ [F5], its spatial cone coordinates satisfy
$$\mathbf k'=\mathbf k+(\gamma-1)(n\cdot\mathbf k)n+\gamma\beta\omega n,\qquad \omega'=\gamma(\omega+\beta n\cdot\mathbf k).$$
Taking $n$ as the third coordinate axis, the first two spatial coordinates are unchanged and
$$\frac{\partial k'_3}{\partial k_3} =\gamma\left(1+\beta\frac{k_3}{\omega}\right)=\frac{\omega'}{\omega}.$$
Thus $\det(\partial\mathbf k'/\partial\mathbf k)=\omega'/\omega$. A rotation has determinant one and preserves $\omega$. By [F2], every proper orthochronous $\Lambda$ is a product of these, so $d^3\mathbf k'/(2\omega')=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega)$. Combining this change of variables with the fiber isometry in step 1.1 proves unitarity on the quotient-section space and verifies the stated identification with $\mathcal H_T$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 Each joint multiplier value $(\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|,-\sum_r\mathbf k_r)$ lies in $\overline V_+$ by the triangle inequality [F9], so the PVM vanishes outside that closed cone. Fix a nonzero $\mathbf k_0$ and the boundary point $(|\mathbf k_0|,-\mathbf k_0)$. Choose $v\in\mathbb R^3$ not parallel to $\mathbf k_0$. By [F7], $P_T(\mathbf k_0)v\ne0$, and continuity gives a bounded open momentum neighborhood $V$ of $\mathbf k_0$, disjoint from zero, on which $\|P_T(\mathbf k)v\|$ is bounded below by a positive constant. Given any open neighborhood $G$ of $(|\mathbf k_0|,-\mathbf k_0)$, shrink $V$ so the map $\mathbf k\mapsto(|\mathbf k|,-\mathbf k)$ sends $V$ into $G$. Choose a ball inside $V$ and a positive finite-measure box $Q$ inside that ball by [F8]. The vector $u(\mathbf k)=\mathbf1_Q(\mathbf k)P_T(\mathbf k)v$ is a nonzero element of $\mathcal H_T$ supported over $G$, so $\mathsf E(G)u=u\ne0$. The vacuum supplies the origin. [A1, F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, step 1.2, given, construct]

3.1 Matrix multiplication is continuous, and the Lorentz equation gives $\Lambda^{-1}=\eta\Lambda^T\eta$, so inversion is continuous in the stated matrix topology. For $v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with support in $B_R$, $R\ge1$, take the four-component representative $s_v(p)=(0,\sqrt{2\omega}\,P_T(\mathbf k)v(\mathbf k))$; under the stated unitary identification its class corresponds to $u=P_Tv\in\mathcal H_T$. Put $q=\Lambda^{-1}p$ and $a_\Lambda(\mathbf k)=T_p\Lambda(0,\sqrt{2q^0}\,P_T(\mathbf q)v(\mathbf q))$, the transverse chart representative of the transformed quotient section. If $\Lambda$ is sufficiently close to $I$, uniformly for future null $p$ one has $\omega/2\le q^0=|\mathbf q|\le2\omega$ and $\|\Lambda\|_{\rm op}\le2$: use $\|p\|_2=\sqrt2\omega$, the displayed inverse formula and the Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz bound for a matrix acting on a vector. Thus $a_\Lambda$ vanishes outside $B_{2R}$, and $\|T_p\|_{\rm op}\le\sqrt2$, $\|P_T\|_{\rm op}\le1$ give $|a_\Lambda(\mathbf k)|\le C M\sqrt\omega$, where $M=\sup|v|$ and $C$ is independent of sufficiently small $\Lambda-I$. Consequently $|a_\Lambda-a_I|$ is bounded by a fixed constant $C_R M$ on the common support. Its squared $L^2(d\nu)$ contribution on $B_\delta$ is at most $C_R^2M^2\nu(B_\delta)=C_R^2M^2\pi\delta^2$ by [F6, F10]. On the annulus $\delta\le|\mathbf k|\le2R$, extend the explicit formula to matrices $A$ in a sufficiently small closed Euclidean matrix box about $I$ by putting $q=\eta A^T\eta p$. On that box $q^0$ and $|\mathbf q|$ remain positive, bounded away from zero on the annulus; the formula using $P_T(\mathbf q)=I-(\mathbf q/|\mathbf q|)(\mathbf q/|\mathbf q|)^T$ is therefore continuous. The box times annulus is closed bounded in $\mathbb R^{19}$, hence compact, and [F11] gives uniform continuity of this formula there. Restricting back to Lorentz matrices yields $a_\Lambda\to a_I$ uniformly on the annulus, which has finite $\nu$-measure by [F6]. First choose $\delta$, then $\Lambda-I$, to obtain $\|a_\Lambda-a_I\|_{L^2(d\nu)}\to0$; this is exactly the quotient-section norm. No fiber value at the omitted apex is used. These sections are dense by [F4, F7]: approximate any $u\in\mathcal H_T$ by smooth compactly supported $v$ and project by $P_T$. Unitarity from step 2.1 gives $\|U_\Lambda s-s\|\le2\|s-s_v\|+\|U_\Lambda s_v-s_v\|$, extending continuity to every section. At any $\Lambda_0$, the representation identity reduces continuity to $U_{\Lambda_0^{-1}\Lambda}\to I$, and $\Lambda_0^{-1}\Lambda\to I$ in the matrix topology. For an elementary $n$-tensor, telescoping and unitarity give $\|(U_\Lambda^{\otimes n}-I)(h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_n)\|\le\sum_{j=1}^n\|(U_\Lambda-I)h_j\|\prod_{l\ne j}\|h_l\|\to0$. Finite linear combinations are dense in the Hilbert tensor product; the symmetric projection is a contraction commuting with the tensor action, so continuity holds on each symmetric sector. The vacuum is fixed. Truncating an arbitrary Fock vector to finitely many sectors leaves an error bounded by twice its tail norm under these unitary maps; letting that tail tend to zero proves strong continuity on all Fock space. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Fix $(E,\mathbf P)$ with $E>|\mathbf P|$. Choose a unit $n\perp\mathbf P$; if $\mathbf P\ne0$, select a standard basis vector $w$ not parallel to $\mathbf P$ and normalize $w-(w\cdot\mathbf P/|\mathbf P|^2)\mathbf P$, while if $\mathbf P=0$ take any standard basis vector. Put $q=\tfrac12\sqrt{E^2-|\mathbf P|^2}$ and let $\mathbf k_1=-\mathbf P/2+qn$, $\mathbf k_2=-\mathbf P/2-qn$. Since $n\cdot\mathbf P=0$, $|\mathbf k_i|^2=|\mathbf P|^2/4+q^2=E^2/4$, so they are distinct nonzero momenta with $|\mathbf k_1|+|\mathbf k_2|=E$ and $-(\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2)=\mathbf P$. Given any open neighborhood $G$ of $(E,\mathbf P)$, continuity of the two-particle sum map gives disjoint bounded momentum neighborhoods $V_1,V_2$ of $\mathbf k_1,\mathbf k_2$ whose pairwise sums map into $G$. Choose fixed $v_i$ not parallel to $\mathbf k_i$ and shrink $V_i$ so $P_T(\mathbf k)v_i$ never vanishes there by [F7]; choose balls inside $V_i$ and positive finite-measure boxes $Q_i$ inside those balls by [F8]. The vectors $u_i(\mathbf k)=\mathbf1_{Q_i}(\mathbf k)P_T(\mathbf k)v_i$ are nonzero in $\mathcal H_T$. The symmetric vector $\Psi_2=P_{s,2}(u_1\otimes u_2)$ is nonzero because $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are disjoint, and its two-particle multiplier values lie in $G$. Hence $\mathsf E(G)\Psi_2=\Psi_2\ne0$. Thus every neighborhood of $(E,\mathbf P)$ has nonzero two-particle spectral projection. Together with steps 1.2–2.2 this proves $\operatorname{supp}(\mathsf E)=\overline V_+$; [F3] gives the exact energy domain from step 1.2. [A1, F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 2.2, given, construct] ∎
